questions.question: A byte-addressable machine has a 32-bit address. It has a 64 KB direct-mapped cache with a block size of 32 bytes. Find the number of bits in the TAG, LINE (index), and WORD (offset) fields.
questions.solutionApproach: offset = log2(32) = 5 bits. #lines = 64KB/32B = 2048 = 2^11 → index = 11 bits. tag = 32 − 5 − 11 = 16 bits.
questions.answer: TAG = 16 bits, LINE = 11 bits, WORD = 5 bits

questions.question: Same machine as above, but now the cache is 4-way set-associative instead of direct-mapped, with the same total cache size and block size. Find the new SET index width and TAG width.
questions.solutionApproach: #lines unchanged = 2048. #sets = 2048/4 = 512 = 2^9 → set index = 9 bits. tag = 32 − 5 − 9 = 18 bits.
questions.answer: SET = 9 bits, TAG = 18 bits (associativity increase always shrinks index bits and grows tag bits, for fixed cache size)

questions.question: A system has L1 (hit time 1 ns, local miss rate 8%) and L2 (hit time 8 ns, local miss rate 25%) caches, and main memory access time 100 ns. Compute the AMAT.
questions.solutionApproach: Work backward: AMAT_L2 = 8 + 0.25×100 = 33 ns. AMAT_L1 = 1 + 0.08×33 = 3.64 ns.

questions.question: A fully associative cache with 3 lines (initially empty) uses LRU. Reference sequence (block numbers): 1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5. How many misses occur?
questions.solutionApproach: 1(miss,[1]) 2(miss,[1,2]) 3(miss,[1,2,3],full) 1(hit,reorder→[2,3,1]) 4(miss,evict LRU=2→[3,1,4]) 2(miss,evict LRU=3→[1,4,2]) 5(miss,evict LRU=1→[4,2,5]). Misses = 1,2,3,4,2,5 → 6 misses, 1 hit.

questions.question: A 100x100 array of 4-byte integers is stored row-major. Cache block size = 32 bytes, direct-mapped, large enough to ignore conflict misses. Compare cache misses for row-major traversal (i outer, j inner) vs column-major traversal (j outer, i inner) over the full array.
questions.solutionApproach: Elements per block = 32/4 = 8. Row-major: consecutive j accesses hit 7 out of every 8 → misses ≈ 10000/8 = 1250. Column-major: consecutive i accesses jump 400 bytes each time (never same block) → every access is a miss ≈ 10000.
questions.answer: Row-major ≈ 1250 misses; Column-major ≈ 10000 misses (8x more) — demonstrates why loop order matters.

questions.question: Which of the following is/are TRUE? (MSQ style) (A) Write-back caches require a dirty bit. (B) Write-through caches never need a dirty bit. (C) A write-back cache always generates less memory bus traffic than a write-through cache for a given workload. (D) Inclusion property requires that every block in L2 also be present in L1.
questions.solutionApproach: (A) True — need to track which lines differ from memory. (B) True — memory is always up to date. (C) True generally (fewer writes propagate) — mark true for a standard workload. (D) FALSE — inclusion is the other way: L1 ⊆ L2, not L2 ⊆ L1. This is the classic reversal trap.
questions.answer: A, B, C are true; D is false (reversed direction — classic GATE trap).
